The result is a dizzying labyrinth of carved cedar ceilings, geometric plasterwork, and reflecting pools that still serves as the official Seville residence of the Spanish royal family.
095.p2: Getting inside Pedro's masterpiece requires navigating a courtyard entry line outside the Lion's Gate that bakes under the Andalusian sun like an unglazed terracotta pot. By mid-afternoon in July, temperatures in Seville regularly pass a hundred and five degrees, driving perspiring crowds into the narrow arched galleries where tour guides wave colored umbrellas and argue in five languages over who gets to stand beneath the dome of the Hall of Ambassadors. Once you finally escape to the sprawling gardens, you are immediately accosted by resident peacocks that shriek like rusty hinges and aggressively stalk anyone holding a paper bag from a bakery.
095.p3: None of the intricate azulejo tilework could console @CasseroleCritique, who penned "A Royal Mess of a Meal!" to complain about "layers of lukewarm ingredients" and the shocking absence of an all-you-can-eat casserole. One can only assume that jet lag and extreme Iberian heat stroke caused this traveler to read "Alcázar" on a tourist brochure and hear "All-Casserole," prompting them to show up at the oldest royal palace in active use in Europe with a Tupperware container and a serving spoon. If you find yourself chewing on anything lukewarm in the Courtyard of the Maidens, you are probably eating sixteenth-century lime mortar.
095.visitor_tip: Book the first timed entry slot of the morning weeks in advance on the official website, and bring a handheld fan if you visit between May and September.

096.headline: Three Hundred Billion Trees, Two Million Insect Species, and Not a Single Frontal Lobe in Sight
096.p1: When Spanish conquistador Francisco de Orellana drifted down the world's largest river system by volume in 1541, his chronicler Friar Gaspar de Carvajal claimed their starving party was attacked by tall female warriors resembling the Amazons of Greek myth, giving the whole basin its enduring name. What Orellana had stumbled into was a two-point-seven-million-square-mile biological engine draining forty percent of South America and discharging enough fresh water into the Atlantic Ocean to dilute the sea's salinity more than a hundred miles from shore. Far from being untouched primeval wilderness, recent lidar scans have revealed that pre-Columbian civilizations built vast networks of causeways, earthen mounds, and orchards in the dark soil before European diseases decimated their populations in the sixteenth century.
096.p2: Experiencing the Brazilian Amazon today usually begins in Manaus, a humid metropolis of two million people where an nineteenth-century rubber-boom opera house sits surrounded by dense tropical forest. From there, travelers board wooden riverboats or floatplanes to jungle lodges where the air feels like a wet wool blanket wrapped around your face. Every walk requires knee-high rubber boots to guard against pit vipers and bullet ants whose sting feels like taking a nail gun to the shin. At night, the forest floor erupts into a deafening chorus of tree frogs and howler monkeys that sounds like a small aircraft engine starting up directly outside your mosquito net.
096.p3: Yet @GreyMatterTraveler somehow emerged from the basin complaining of "Overthinking this 'natural' wonder!", noting in their review that they "found only tangled thoughts near that big river" and that their "cerebral cortex is drenched... but not with rain!" Travelling thousands of miles up the Rio Negro because you misheard "Amazon Rainforest" as "Amazon Brainforest" is a neurological puzzle in its own right. While the meandering tributaries of the floodplains certainly look like cerebral blood vessels from an airplane window, expecting actual grey matter to hang from the kapok trees suggests our reviewer may have forgotten to take their malaria prophylaxis on schedule.
096.visitor_tip: Pack lightweight long-sleeved synthetic clothing rather than cotton, seal your electronics inside dry bags, and always shake out your rubber boots before putting your feet in.

097.headline: Two and a Half Miles of Portuguese Wave-Patterned Sidewalk and Zero Overripe Potassium
097.p1: Until a tram tunnel was blasted through the coastal granite hills of Rio de Janeiro in 1892, Copacabana was a quiet fishing strip named after a seventeenth-century chapel housing a replica of the Bolivian Virgin of Copacabana. Its transformation into an international playground began in 1906, when Mayor Francisco Pereira Passos imported Portuguese craftsmen to lay down the famous black-and-white basalt and limestone mosaic promenade, designed in flowing waves to honor the meeting of the Atlantic Ocean and the shore. When the white stucco Copacabana Palace hotel opened in 1923, European royalty and Hollywood stars flocked south to gamble, though the beach itself was so narrow that high tides regularly flooded Avenida Atlântica until engineers pumped millions of cubic yards of offshore sand onto the coast in 1970.
097.p2: Modern Copacabana is a two-and-a-half-mile theater of high-velocity recreation and relentless commerce. Divided into numbered lifeguard stations called postos, the sand is packed wall-to-wall with rental umbrellas, locals playing footvolley with physics-defying chest passes, and tourists wearing far too little sunscreen. You cannot sit on a towel for ninety seconds without being approached by a procession of whistling vendors selling grilled queijo coalho cheese over live charcoal cans, iced mate tea from plastic barrels, silk sarongs, and suspiciously cheap sunglasses. Meanwhile, the Atlantic shorebreak delivers deceptive dumper waves capable of tumbling an inattentive swimmer like laundry in a heavy spin cycle.
097.p3: Into this lively coastal scene stepped @SlipperySam, who rated the landmark one star in "This place is rotten!" after encountering "a slippery, yellow, curved nightmare" where they could only build "fruit piles" instead of sandcastles. Confusing Copacabana Beach with a giant banana peel takes an extraordinary commitment to slapstick comedy, even if Barry Manilow's song never explicitly clarified the absence of plantains. Unless @SlipperySam accidentally wandered into the loading dock of a municipal wholesale produce market in northern Rio, blaming a four-kilometer Atlantic sandbar for melting your tanning lotion in a heap of bruised fruit is pure tropical delusion.
097.visitor_tip: Leave your jewelry and expensive watch in the hotel safe, buy a fresh coconut at a boardwalk kiosk, and never take your eyes off the heavy shorebreak when wading in.

098.headline: Fifteen Hundred Years of Bone-Dry Peruvian Geoglyphs That Will Not Garnish Your Margarita
098.p1: Between roughly 500 BCE and 500 CE, the Nazca people of southern Peru created hundreds of giant geometric lines and animal figures across a barren coastal plateau using a technique that required almost no heavy engineering. By scraping away twelve to fifteen inches of dark, iron-oxide-coated pebbles to expose the pale, high-lime clay soil underneath, they drew hummingbirds, monkeys, spiders, and killer whales measuring up to twelve hundred feet long. Because the Pampa Colorada plain receives less than twenty minutes of rain per year and sits sheltered from wind by a warm air cushion, the shallow trenches stayed intact for centuries. After being largely ignored until commercial pilots spotted them in the 1920s, the lines were mapped obsessively by German mathematician Maria Reiche, who spent forty years sweeping the desert with a broom from atop an aluminum step-ladder.
098.p2: Seeing these ancient drawings today is essentially an exercise in controlled motion sickness. While a roadside metal observation tower along the Pan-American Highway lets you view two figures (the Tree and the Hands) for the price of a few soles, the rest require boarding a tiny six-seat Cessna at the local aerodrome. To make sure passengers on both sides of the cabin get a photograph of the nine-hundred-foot Condor or the strange round-eyed Astronaut, the pilots bank their wings at steep forty-five-degree angles in tight figure-eights over the thermal updrafts. Half the passengers spend the thirty-minute flight staring intently at two-thousand-year-old ceremonial paths while the other half stare intently into white paper airsick bags.
098.p3: Apparently, @CitrusScribbler skipped the Cessna altogether and went straight for the produce aisle, writing "Warning: Extreme Pucker Factor!" to complain about "incredibly sour, tiny green things everywhere" and sticky juice obscuring the viewing platform. Traveling six hours south of Lima down the desert coast expecting the Nazca Lines to be the "Nazca Limes" is a heroic failure of reading comprehension. There is no lime juice on the Pampa de San José; in fact, stepping onto the protected pebbles without government authorization is a felony in Peru, as Greenpeace activists infamously discovered in 2014.
098.visitor_tip: Take a motion-sickness pill an hour before boarding the sightseeing plane, eat a very light breakfast, and keep both cameras ready when the pilot tips the wing.

099.headline: Fourteen Thousand Miles of Galvanized Steel Wire Spanning the East River With Zero Dietary Fiber
099.p1: When the Brooklyn Bridge opened on May 24, 1883, its sixteen-hundred-foot main span was the longest suspension bridge on earth and the first to use steel wire instead of iron. The project nearly destroyed the Roebling family: chief designer John Augustus Roebling died of tetanus in 1869 after a ferry crushed his toes during surveying, and his son Washington Roebling suffered debilitating decompression sickness (then called caissons disease) after spending hours inside pressurized underwater wooden boxes at the river bottom. Confined to his Brooklyn Heights bedroom, Washington supervised the rest of the fourteen-year construction through a telescope, relying on his wife, Emily Warren Roebling, who mastered higher mathematics and catenary curve engineering to manage the contractors and become the first person to cross the finished bridge.
099.p2: Crossing Emily and Washington's triumph today is less a romantic nineteenth-century promenade and more an obstacle course in high-altitude urban survival. Although the city finally banished cyclists to a separate lane on the lower roadway in 2021, the elevated wooden pedestrian boardwalk remains packed shoulder-to-shoulder with tourists stopping abruptly in the middle of traffic to pose beneath the pointed Gothic limestone arches. Between the rumble of six lanes of commuter cars humming beneath the floorboards, street vendors hawking plastic Statue of Liberty crowns, and wedding photographers commanding twenty-foot exclusion zones in the wind, getting the mile from Manhattan's City Hall to DUMBO takes forty-five minutes and saintly patience.
099.p3: For @GreenerPastures, however, the real problem was culinary, as detailed in their review "A total cruciferous nightmare!", which griped that the cables were "just fibrous stems" forming a "giant, soggy vegetable span." It takes a rare dietary fixation to walk onto a landmark supported by four fifteen-inch-thick galvanized steel cables and mistake them for overcooked stalks of broccoli. Funnily enough, a crooked wire contractor named J. Lloyd Haigh actually did smuggle defective, brittle steel wire into the bridge's spinning wheels in 1878 before getting caught, though even Haigh never tried substituting fresh produce for high-tensile carbon steel.
099.visitor_tip: Walk from the Brooklyn side toward Manhattan at sunrise so the skyline is directly in front of you and the midday crowds are still asleep in their hotels.

100.headline: Nineteen Volcanic Islands Full of Unbothered Reptiles and Not a Single Thoroughbred Racehorse
100.p1: Sitting six hundred miles off the coast of Ecuador astride the equator, the Galápagos archipelago was discovered purely by accident in 1535 when the ship carrying Fray Tomás de Berlanga, the Bishop of Panama, drifted off course in dead calm winds. His crew nearly died of thirst chewing prickly pear cactus pads and wrote back to King Charles V that the islands looked as though God had rained volcanic stones upon the earth. For three centuries the jagged lava fields served primarily as a hideout for English buccaneers and a pantry for nineteenth-century whalers, who stacked live giant tortoises in their ships' holds because the reptiles could survive for a year without food or water. When a twenty-six-year-old Charles Darwin arrived aboard HMS Beagle in 1835, it was the local vice-governor who casually mentioned that you could tell which island a tortoise came from by the shape of its shell.
100.p2: Visiting the archipelago today is an exercise in strict biosecurity and comical wildlife dodging. Before boarding a flight from Quito or Guayaquil, your luggage is x-rayed and fumigated to prevent a single mainland seed from sneaking onto Santa Cruz or San Cristóbal. Once ashore, national park rules require an accredited naturalist guide and a rigorous six-foot buffer from all animals, a law the animals themselves completely ignore. Sea lions sprawl across wooden passenger benches, marine iguanas sneeze thick crusts of sea salt onto the boardwalks while basking in piles like miniature dinosaurs, and blue-footed boobies conduct elaborate high-stepping mating dances directly in the middle of the footpath.
100.p3: This evolutionary paradise was deemed a total bust by @GallopGrunt, whose review, "A real neigh-mare!", fumed that the islands were "Ecuador's worst stable" and complained about the "constant thunder of hooves" agitating the tortoises. How someone pays the two-hundred-dollar Galápagos National Park entry tax expecting the "Gallop-A-Go Islands" to be an offshore Kentucky Derby track is a mystery that would have stumped Darwin himself. Considering that the resident giant tortoises top out at a brisk zero-point-two miles per hour when motivated by fresh leaves, anyone hearing thundering hooves on the lava rock should probably drink more water and get out of the equatorial sun.
100.visitor_tip: Bring plenty of US cash in crisp twenties since island ATMs frequently run empty, and always check dark dock steps at night before stepping on a sleeping sea lion.

101.headline: Five Hundred Million Liters of Zambezi River Per Minute and Zero Free-Range Poultry
101.p1: Long before Scottish missionary David Livingstone was paddled to the brink of the Zambezi River's great chasm in 1855 and dutifully named it after his reigning monarch, the local Kololo and Toka-Leya peoples called the cataract Mosi-oa-Tunya, or "The Smoke That Thunders." The name is entirely literal: here, the placid, mile-wide Zambezi abruptly plunges over the edge of a flat basalt plateau into a transverse fissure less than two hundred feet across and three hundred and fifty-four feet deep. Because the entire volume of the river is compressed into a narrow zig-zagging gorge carved out of ancient volcanic fractures, the impact sends a permanent column of spray sixteen hundred feet into the air, visible from thirty miles away across the dry woodland of Zambia and Zimbabwe.
101.p2: What your experience of Victoria Falls looks like depends entirely on which month you show up and how much you enjoy walking through an automatic car wash with your clothes on. At peak flood in April and May, five hundred million liters of water cascade over the lip every sixty seconds, generating an upward rainstorm along the Knife-Edge Bridge that penetrates every known brand of waterproof jacket within ten seconds. Conversely, if you visit the Zambian side at the end of the dry season in November, the Eastern Cataract slows to a polite trickle over bare black basalt, leaving tourists to peer into dry rock pools while cheeky Chacma baboons raid unattended backpacks near the curio stalls.
101.p3: None of this hydrological power satisfied @CluckyCritic, who titled their review "Total Bird-en!" and complained of finding "noisy, clucking avian chaos" and "endless bird droppings" instead of a waterfall. Showing up on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe expecting "Victoria's Fowls" to be a regal Victorian chicken coop is an ambitious geographical error, even for the internet. While the cliffs of the Batoka Gorge do host rare Taita falcons and black eagles, anyone standing beside the largest curtain of falling water on the planet and complaining about barnyard poultry has taken a very wrong turn at Livingstone airport.
101.visitor_tip: Put your phone and passport inside a sealed zip-top bag before walking the rainforest path, and bring crisp US bills issued after 2013 for the KAZA Univisa at the border.

102.headline: Five Hundred Years of Secret New Kingdom Royal Tombs That Were Never a Costume Jewelry Mall
102.p1: Around 1500 BCE, the pharaohs of Egypt's Eighteenth Dynasty came to the sensible realization that building giant triangular stone pyramids on the flat desert horizon was basically putting up a neon billboard for grave robbers. Starting with Thutmose I, royal architects relocated the state cemetery across the Nile from Thebes (modern Luxor) into a remote, sun-baked limestone wadi on the west bank called the Valley of the Kings. For nearly five centuries, an elite village of state artisans lived in nearby Deir el-Medina, chiseling secret subterranean corridors up to four hundred feet into the mountain rock and painting the walls with vivid guides to the underworld, only for corrupt necropolis priests and ancient looters to strip almost every single tomb bare before the Roman era.
102.p2: Visiting the sixty-three known tombs today is like stepping into an archaeological convection oven. Because the Theban Hills trap solar radiation against pale limestone rock, summer temperatures on the valley floor routinely pass a hundred and fifteen degrees in the shade, and there is no shade. After riding an electric tram from the visitor center, tourists queue at the narrow stone stairways descending into the earth, where the combined body heat and exhalations of hundreds of people make the air thick enough to slice. Inside, local guardians in galabiyas gesture toward ceiling paintings of the sky goddess Nut and softly offer to let you take forbidden flash photographs in exchange for small-denomination Egyptian banknotes.
102.p3: Somehow, @TackyTreasureHunter descended into this three-thousand-year-old royal burial ground expecting a discount Claire's boutique, leaving a review titled "More like Valley of the Crings!" that griped about "cheap rhinestones" and "gaudy, fake jewels." It is true that if you went looking for King Tutankhamun's twenty-four-pound solid gold burial mask inside his modest tomb (KV62), you missed it by about a century; Howard Carter packed the five thousand artefacts off to Cairo after his 1922 discovery, leaving only Tut's actual linen-wrapped mummy behind in a climate-controlled glass box. Calling thirty-three-century-old mineral pigments on carved limestone "plastic bling," however, is a felony against art history.
102.visitor_tip: Arrive at six in the morning when the gates open to beat both the tour buses from the Red Sea and the midday heat, and pay the extra ticket fee for the spectacularly preserved tomb of Seti I.

103.headline: Seven Centuries of Baltic Cobblestones and Tilted Merchants' Houses With Zero Chewing Gum
103.p1: Founded around 1252 by the Swedish statesman Birger Jarl as a fortified padlock between Lake Mälaren and the Baltic Sea, Stockholm's Gamla Stan sits across three rocky islands where the streets are still laid out according to their medieval footprints. During the Middle Ages, German Hanseatic merchants packed the island of Stadsholmen with tall, narrow brick houses painted in warm ochre, dandelion yellow, and rust red, hoisting cargo into upper-story attics with iron pulleys that still jut from the gables today. In November 1520, the central square of Stortorget hosted the infamous Stockholm Bloodbath, where the newly crowned Danish King Christian II invited eighty Swedish nobles to a three-day coronation banquet and then promptly had them all beheaded on the cobblestones outside.
103.p2: Modern Stortorget is considerably less lethal, though your wallet may feel otherwise if you sit down for a twenty-dollar cinnamon bun and filter coffee at an outdoor table. Because the medieval alleys were built for handcarts rather than cruise-ship excursions, summer crowds bottleneck along Västerlånggatan, shuffling past shops stocked to the rafters with plastic Viking helmets, stuffed plush moose, and Dala horses. When travelers inevitably squeeze into Mårten Trotzigs Gränd, an alley that narrows to just thirty-five inches wide at the top of its thirty-six steps, it takes only one person stopping to tie a shoelace to cause a twenty-minute pedestrian gridlock.
103.p3: Yet @StickySole came away from Sweden's historic heart with a bizarrely literal grievance, writing in "My Nordic Nightmare Was Sweet and Gross!" that their boots were "glued to what felt like ancient Scandinavian candy" and that the district merely dispenses "round, colorful orbs." Mistaking "Gamla Stan" (which simply means "The Old Town" in Swedish) for "Gumball Stan" requires a heroic indifference to geography and dental hygiene. The round objects embedded in the corners of the medieval buildings are not jawbreakers; they are iron cannonballs and seventeenth-century boundary stones designed to protect the brickwork from wagon wheels, and you should definitely stop trying to chew on them.
103.visitor_tip: Avoid the souvenir-choked main drag of Västerlånggatan and wander one block east to Österlånggatan or Prästgatan, where you can still see sixteenth-century iron wall braces in quiet peace.

104.headline: Forty Thousand Square Miles of Hyper-Arid Chilean Salt Flats and Not a Single Corn Tortilla
104.p1: Wedged between the cold Humboldt Current of the Pacific Ocean and the towering volcanic wall of the Andes, Chile's Atacama Desert sits inside a double rain shadow so severe that several weather stations have never recorded a single drop of precipitation in human history. Soil samples from the central Yungay core are so completely devoid of organic moisture and microbial life that NASA uses the plateau as a stand-in for testing Mars rovers before launching them into space. For over a century, the region's one commercial advantage was its thick crust of sodium nitrate, or "white gold," which sparked the 1879 War of the Pacific against Peru and Bolivia before German chemists invented synthetic fertilizer and turned dozens of desert mining camps into wind-scoured ghost towns.
104.p2: Today, travelers base themselves in the adobe oasis village of San Pedro de Atacama, where the elevation starts at eight thousand feet and the relative humidity frequently dips below five percent. Within forty-eight hours, every visitor develops chapped lips, static-charged hair that stands straight up, and nasal passages dry enough to strike a match on. Tourists wake at four in the morning in sub-freezing darkness to bounce up to the El Tatio geyser field at fourteen thousand feet, shivering in down parkas beside boiling mud pots before descending by afternoon to the Valle de la Luna, where the salt crust literally crackles and pops in the ninety-degree heat as the sun sets.
104.p3: Into this planetary furnace wandered @DryTortilla, who left a furious one-star review titled "Where's the flavor?!" after driving across northern Chile and finding "just sand and zero tacos" in what they assumed was the "A Taco Mama Desert." It takes an extraordinary dedication to Mexican street food to fly to the driest non-polar desert on the planet expecting a roadside taqueria behind every salt dune. While @DryTortilla was technically accurate in observing that their tortilla chips grew stale from the lack of moisture, blaming a fifteen-million-year-old hyper-arid plateau for not serving carne asada with extra cilantro is a tough break for the Chilean tourism board.
104.visitor_tip: Drink at least four liters of water a day, pack saline nasal spray and heavy lip balm, and avoid booking high-altitude geyser excursions on your very first morning in town.

105.headline: Thirteen Thousand Miles of Ming Dynasty Brick and Sticky-Rice Mortar That Will Not Make Wine
105.p1: First, let us clear up two durable myths: the Great Wall of China is not a single unbroken rampart, and you cannot see it from the moon with the naked eye unless your eyesight is good enough to spot a highway lane from two hundred and forty thousand miles away. What actually stretches for roughly thirteen thousand miles across northern China is a sprawling network of overlapping walls, trenches, and watchtowers built across two millennia. While China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, linked early rammed-earth fortifications in the third century BCE using hundreds of thousands of conscripted laborers, the dramatic crenellated brick battlements tourists climb north of Beijing today were built during the Ming Dynasty between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries, bound together with a surprisingly resilient mortar made of slaked lime and sticky rice.
105.p2: Climbing a Ming Dynasty mountain ridge in the twenty-first century is a vertical workout disguised as sightseeing. Because the stairs were designed to slow down invading Mongol cavalry rather than accommodate human knees, the stone risers vary wildly from two inches high to two feet tall on a forty-five-degree incline. At the popular Badaling section, forty-five miles from central Beijing, holiday crowds pack the walkway so tightly that nobody actually walks; you simply shuffle forward in a slow human conveyor belt until you reach a watchtower, take a sweaty photograph in the smog, and pay extra to ride a stainless-steel toboggan slide back down the mountain to a parking lot lined with KFC franchises.
105.p3: None of this defensive masonry impressed @SourGrape, whose review, "More like a 'Great' Disappointment!", complained of "sticky... purple stains" and insisted the monument was "just a trellis holding up a mess" of fruit pulp. One struggles to imagine the travel agent who booked @SourGrape a flight to Beijing to visit the "Grape Wall of China," let alone how a tourist scaled a twenty-five-foot granite and grey-brick parapet along the Yanshan Mountains expecting a Napa Valley merlot harvest. If you found purple stains on the stones at Mutianyu, someone ahead of you simply dropped an overpriced mulberry popsicle on the steps.
105.visitor_tip: Skip the crush at Badaling in favor of the Mutianyu or Jinshanling sections, wear shoes with serious rubber grip for the steep polished stones, and take the chairlift up.

106.headline: Twenty-Five-Ton Neolithic Sarsen Megaliths on Salisbury Plain That Have Never Swung Open
106.p1: Constructed in stages between 3000 BCE and 1500 BCE by Neolithic Britons who lacked both the wheel and metal tools, Stonehenge is a masterclass in prehistoric stubbornness. While the outer twenty-five-ton sarsen sandstone blocks were dragged on timber sledges from the Marlborough Downs twenty miles away, eighty smaller bluestones were somehow hauled a hundred and forty miles from the Preseli Hills in western Wales. What few tourists realize is that the monument was heavily tidied up in the twentieth century: after philanthropist Cecil Chubb bought the circle at a 1915 auction on a whim for sixty-six hundred pounds and gave it to the nation, engineers spent the 1950s using mobile cranes and concrete foundations to straighten leaning pillars and re-seat fallen lintels.
106.p2: Visiting the Salisbury Plain today begins a mile and a half west of the stones at a sleek visitor center, where crowds line up in a damp Wiltshire crosswind for diesel shuttle buses. Unless you pay extra for a special dawn access tour, a low rope barrier keeps you thirty yards away from the actual circle, ensuring that your experience consists of walking a slow loop on a paved path while listening to an audio guide describe solstice alignments. Just a couple of hundred yards away, a perpetual queue of heavy lorries and campervans crawls along the single-lane A303 highway, providing a picturesque backdrop of brake lights to five thousand years of Neolithic mystery.
106.p3: That rope barrier was the least of the problems for @WobblyJoint, who filed "This place is utterly unhinged!" to complain that the giant stones "don't even open" and offer "zero entrance/exit functionality." Driving two hours west of London to inspect "Stone Hinge" as if it were a colossal Bronze Age hardware showroom is a triumph of literal-minded disappointment. It is true that the horizontal lintels are locked onto the upright pillars using woodworker-style mortise-and-tenon joints carved directly into the rock, which is impressive carpentry for 2500 BCE, even if none of the thirty-ton trilithons pivot open when you push on them.
106.visitor_tip: Skip the crowded shuttle bus and walk the mile and a half from the visitor center across the open National Trust chalk downland through the prehistoric Cursus barrow cemetery.

107.headline: Twelve Thousand Feet of Basalt Ash and Dormant Volcanic Fury That Cannot Be Eaten With a Spoon
107.p1: Japan's highest peak is actually three volcanoes stacked on top of one another like geological nesting dolls, capped by the symmetrical cone of Shin-Fuji, which has been piling up basaltic lava and scoria for the last ten thousand years. Its most recent temper tantrum occurred in December 1707, when the Hoei eruption blasted eighty million cubic meters of volcanic ash across Edo (modern Tokyo) sixty miles away, darkening the midday sky and burying villages ten feet deep in black cinders. Revered for centuries by Shinto and Buddhist ascetics as a sacred dwelling of fire deities, Mount Fuji barred women from its upper slopes until 1868, when Lady Fanny Parkes, the wife of the British ambassador, marched to the summit in ankle-length Victorian skirts.
107.p2: For ten months of the year, Mount Fuji is a snowy, wind-blasted ice cone best admired from the window of a Shinkansen bullet train, assuming the notorious summer cloud bank hasn't hidden the entire mountain behind grey fog. During the official July-to-September climbing season, however, four hundred thousand hikers converge on the Yoshida Trail, paying a mandatory two-thousand-yen toll at the fifth station before shuffling upward through loose, knee-deep volcanic gravel. By two in the morning, the upper switchbacks turn into a nose-to-tail conga line of glowing headlamps inching toward the crater rim in sub-zero gusts, while climbers pay a thousand yen to use bio-toilets and buy canned oxygen at mountainside huts.
107.p3: None of this volcanic grit deterred @SugarShocked, whose review, "An Edible Catastrophe!", expressed outrage at finding no chocolatey dessert atop "Mound Fudgey." If you climb to twelve thousand three hundred and eighty-eight feet expecting a three-hundred-year-old stratovolcano to be a towering heap of warm chocolate fudge, the ensuing disappointment is entirely on you. In summer, when the snowcap melts completely away, the bare upper slopes of reddish-brown and black volcanic scoria really do look a bit like a stale brownie from a distance, though biting into a chunk of porous Pleistocene basalt will ruin your dental work much faster than sugar ever could.
107.visitor_tip: If you want to actually see the snow-capped peak clearly, visit the Five Lakes region on a crisp morning in December or January rather than during the cloudy summer climbing season.

108.headline: Two Million Acres of Boiling Acid Springs and Cranky Bison That Make a Terrible Headrest
108.p1: When mountain man John Colter walked out of the Wyoming wilderness in 1808 and described spouting fountains of boiling water and bubbling pits of sulfurous mud, East Coast newspapers laughed it off as "Colter's Hell" and assumed he was delirious. Not until the 1871 Hayden Geological Survey brought back photographs and paintings did Congress believe the stories, prompting President Ulysses S. Grant to sign legislation in 1872 creating Yellowstone as the world's first national park. What sits beneath the park's pine forests is actually an active supervolcano caldera thirty miles by forty-five miles wide, where a shallow underground magma chamber superheats groundwater to power more than ten thousand hydrothermal vents and half the planet's active geysers.
108.p2: Navigating this geothermal pressure cooker in July is an exercise in bumper-to-bumper patience. Whenever a solitary bison decides to take an afternoon stroll down the middle of the Grand Loop Road, traffic grinds to a halt for five miles in both directions in what rangers affectionately call a "bison jam." Around the wooden boardwalks of the Upper Geyser Basin and Grand Prismatic Spring, gusts of wind blow clouds of rotten-egg hydrogen sulfide steam directly into tourists' faces while blowing their baseball caps onto the fragile orange bacterial mats. Every summer, at least one visitor ignores the multilingual skull-and-crossbones warning signs to test either the temperature of a two-hundred-degree acidic pool or the patience of a two-thousand-pound bull bison.
108.p3: That lack of softness deeply offended @FlatFluffer, who wrote "Uncushioned Chaos!" to complain that "Pillowstone National Park" was "just a lumpy, unsupportive bed accessory" in constant need of fluffing. Packing your pajamas and driving into the Teton wilderness expecting a volcanic caldera to feel like a goose-down mattress from a department store white sale is a bold misinterpretation of the National Park Service mission. The only thing getting fluffed in the Hayden Valley is the winter coat of a grizzly bear, and attempting to rest your head on either the wildlife or the travertine limestone terraces at Mammoth Hot Springs will end in an airlift to Idaho Falls.
108.visitor_tip: Stay strictly on the wooden boardwalks in all thermal areas, carry EPA-approved bear spray on your hip while hiking, and keep at least twenty-five yards away from every bison.

109.headline: Eight Centuries of Flying Buttresses and Gargoyles on the Île de la Cité With Zero Marinara
109.p1: When Bishop Maurice de Sully ordered the demolition of Paris's cramped fourth-century Romanesque churches in 1163 to build Notre-Dame Cathedral, he launched a construction project that took nearly two hundred years and outlived every architect who worked on it. To keep the thin, hundred-and-fifteen-foot-high stone vaulting from collapsing outward under its own weight, twelfth-century masons pioneered exterior flying buttresses that braced the walls like stone ribs. By the late eighteenth century, however, the cathedral had fallen into such grim disrepair that French Revolutionaries beheaded twenty-eight biblical kings on the facade (mistaking them for French monarchs), melted the bells into cannonballs, and used the nave to store wine barrels until Victor Hugo's 1831 novel shamed the government into hiring Eugène Viollet-le-Duc for a sweeping restoration.
109.p2: Following the catastrophic April 2019 roof fire that toppled Viollet-le-Duc's timber spire, two thousand stonemasons, carpenters, and stained-glass artisans spent five frantic years rebuilding the medieval oak framework by hand with thirteenth-century-style axes before the cathedral's grand reopening in December 2024. Today, the vast parvis plaza outside the triple portals is once again packed with humanity queuing behind metal barriers to pass through airport-style security scanners. While the scrubbed blonde Lutecian limestone inside gleams brighter than it has since the Middle Ages, getting inside without booking a free timed digital reservation days in advance requires standing on the cobblestones alongside brass-band buskers and bold Parisian pigeons for hours.
109.p3: Yet @RamenRambler left the heart of Paris hungry and aggrieved, penning "Total Pasta-trophe!" after somehow getting their rosary beads "tangled in the campanile spaghetti" while gargoyles stared at their lukewarm macaroni at "Noodle Dame Cathedral." Showing up on the banks of the Seine with a fork and a parmesan shaker because you confused a twelfth-century Gothic cathedral with an Italian pastificio is a culinary tragedy worthy of Victor Hugo himself. For the record, the famous horned stone creatures glaring down from the upper gallery are technically chimeras added by Viollet-le-Duc in the 1840s, and they have zero interest in your noodles.
109.visitor_tip: Use the official Notre-Dame mobile app to reserve a free entry time slot two days before your visit, and walk across the Pont de l'Archevêché for the best view of the flying buttresses.

110.headline: Two Miles of Submerged Alder Piles and Renaissance Palazzos That Have Never Hosted Bingo Night
110.p1: Venice's Grand Canal is not actually a man-made ditch; it is the ancient, sweeping S-curve channel of a lagoon river (likely a branch of the Brenta) that early refugees from mainland barbarian invasions lined with mudflats and wooden stakes in the fifth century. Every single marble palazzo facing its two-mile length sits not on bedrock, but on an upside-down forest of millions of alder, oak, and larch tree trunks driven deep into the oxygen-free lagoon clay, where they petrified into stone-like foundations over the centuries. For hundreds of years, the Venetian Republic used the waterway as a theatrical parade route and a giant medieval loading dock, forbidding bridges across it except at the Rialto, where a succession of collapsing wooden spans was finally replaced by Antonio da Ponte's single stone arch in 1591.
110.p2: Riding the length of the canal today on the Line 1 vaporetto waterbus is the world's most scenic contact sport. For nine euros and fifty cents, tourists wedge themselves onto the open bow platform like upright sardines while the boat lurches from dock to dock, churning through green wakes alongside delivery barges, screaming ambulance boats, and fifty-thousand-euro mahogany water taxis. Meanwhile, gondoliers in striped shirts deftly pole groups of stone-faced vacationers past the Ca' d'Oro for ninety euros per half-hour, shouting brisk warnings at reckless kayakers while the damp lagoon breeze carries the unmistakable aroma of low-tide algae and ten-euro takeaway Aperol spritzes.
110.p3: Into this maritime mayhem floated @KnitwitVoyager, who gave the waterway one star in "More like Grumpy Canal!" because their "bingo card got soggy" and they expected "an ancient relative... and a knitting lesson" at the "Granny Canal." One has to admire the sheer commitment of a traveler who flies into Marco Polo Airport, boards a waterbus into a sixth-century lagoon city, and feels cheated that the main thoroughfare isn't a Florida retirement clubhouse serving four-o'clock meatloaf specials. While Venice certainly has plenty of elderly palazzos slowly sinking into the Adriatic silt, none of them will teach you how to purl a cardigan.
110.visitor_tip: Skip the ninety-euro gondola ride and spend two euros to stand across the Grand Canal on a traditional traghetto ferry at Santa Sofia or San Toma just like the locals do.

111.headline: One Hundred and Seventy Acres of Carbonized First-Century Roman Villas That Are Not a Baked Dessert
111.p1: When Mount Vesuvius blew its top in the autumn of 79 CE, the affluent resort town of Pompeii was already mid-way through a decades-long rebuilding program following a devastating earthquake seventeen years earlier. Contrary to popular Hollywood depictions, the city was not drowned in rivers of glowing red liquid lava; instead, it was buried under ten feet of falling white pumice stones for eighteen hours before a series of five-hundred-degree pyroclastic surges of ash and toxic gas suffocated the remaining two thousand residents in seconds. The town vanished so completely from historical memory that locals called the hill simply "La Civita" until 1748, when military engineer Rocque Joaquín de Alcubierre began blasting tunnels through the hardened volcanic tuff to loot bronze statues for the King of Naples.
111.p2: Walking the hundred and seventy acres of excavated streets today is a grueling test of ankle ligaments and sun protection. The ancient Roman carriageways are paved with massive polygonal blocks of volcanic basalt worn deep with chariot ruts, punctuated by raised stone stepping blocks originally placed so togas wouldn't drag through street sewage. There is virtually no shade anywhere between the Forum and the Amphitheatre, and in summer the heat radiates off the stone walls while twenty thousand daily tourists crowd into the tiny, frescoed rooms of the Lupanar brothel to giggle at two-thousand-year-old erotic menu paintings above the stone beds.
111.p3: Yet @CrumblyCrust arrived at the foot of Mount Vesuvius armed with a dessert fork, writing "Definitely Not A-Peeling!" to complain that "Pom-Pie" was "just ashes and old crust" rather than a delicious Italian pastry. Funnily enough, archaeologists have actually excavated eighty-one real carbonized loaves of bread (stamped by first-century bakers like Celer, slave of Quintus Granius Verus) straight out of Pompeii's brick ovens, though after nineteen hundred years in volcanic ash they have the nutritional profile of charcoal briquettes. Demanding flaky pastry crust and fruit filling from the most famous volcanic disaster in human history is a bold way to tour Campania.
111.visitor_tip: Wear thick-soled athletic shoes for the uneven Roman paving stones, bring a reusable bottle to fill at the ancient street fountains (which now supply clean modern drinking water), and take the Circumvesuviana train early.

112.headline: Eight Thousand Feet of Precision Inca Granite Dry-Stone Terraces That Cannot Be Whisked Into a Latte
112.p1: Built around 1450 CE as a royal seasonal estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti and abandoned less than a century later during the Spanish conquest, Machu Picchu managed the neat trick of never being found by the conquistadors at all. Perched on a narrow granite saddle between two jagged peaks high above a hairpin bend of the Urubamba River, roughly sixty percent of the site's construction effort actually lies underground in deep crushed-stone drainage layers that prevent the mountain from sliding into the jungle during torrential Andean rains. When Yale lecturer Hiram Bingham III was led up the slope by local farmer Melchor Arteaga and an eleven-year-old boy named Pablito Alvarez in July 1911, the ceremonial temples were being actively farmed by two resident Peruvian families who were polite enough to offer Bingham a cup of cool water.
112.p2: Getting that same view today requires navigating a bureaucratic labyrinth worthy of an empire. After taking a pricey train to Aguas Calientes and queuing at five in the morning for a fleet of diesel buses that hair-pin up the Hiram Bingham Highway, visitors must choose one of several strictly enforced, one-way walking circuits. You cannot backtrack, you cannot bring a tripod or a walking stick with a metal tip, and there is not a single bathroom inside the archaeological zone once you scan your ticket. Meanwhile, resident llamas casually photobomb tourists in bright plastic ponchos while clouds roll up from the Amazon basin in thirty seconds flat to turn the entire postcard view into a solid wall of white mist.
112.p3: None of this ashlar granite engineering satisfied @SteepedInSorrow, who filed "Definitely Not My Cup of Tea!" after trekking into the Andes for "Matcha Picchu" and complaining that the agricultural terraces produced "a bitter, grainy beverage in the clouds." Mistaking a fifteenth-century Inca citadel in Cusco for an artisanal Japanese green tea bar takes an astronomical amount of phonetic confusion. While local hotel lobbies in Cusco gladly hand out cups of warm coca-leaf tea to stop tourists from passing out from altitude sickness, scraping green lichen off the Temple of the Sun to whisk into a frothy latte will get you permanently deported by Peru's Ministry of Culture.
112.visitor_tip: Spend at least two days acclimatizing in the lower Sacred Valley before your visit, bring your physical passport for entry check, and use the restroom right outside the turnstiles before entering.

113.headline: One Hundred and Two Stories of Indiana Limestone Built in Thirteen Months With Zero Strike Zones
113.p1: Born out of a Roaring Twenties ego contest between General Motors executive John Jakob Raskob and Walter Chrysler over who could build the tallest skyscraper in Manhattan, the Empire State Building went up at a pace that would give a modern OSHA inspector a heart attack. Starting on St. Patrick's Day in 1930, three thousand four hundred ironworkers (including hundreds of Mohawk skywalkers from Kahnawake) riveted fifty-seven thousand tons of steel into place at a rate of four and a half stories per week, finishing the entire hundred-and-two-story tower in just one year and forty-five days. Its famous two-hundred-foot pinnacle was originally designed as a mooring mast for transatlantic zeppelins, an idea quietly abandoned after a single 1931 test where sixty-mile-per-hour updrafts nearly flipped a Navy blimp over Thirty-Fourth Street.
113.p2: When the building opened in May 1931 in the depths of the Great Depression, so many offices sat unrented that New Yorkers mocked it as the "Empty State Building," and the building only stayed solvent thanks to tourists paying a dollar to ride up to the observation deck. Today, that ticket costs between forty-four and seventy-nine dollars, depending on whether you want the open-air eighty-sixth-floor deck or the glass tube on the hundred-and-second floor. Before you ever smell the Midtown breeze, however, you must wind through forty-five minutes of velvet-rope velvet mazes, mandatory green-screen photo booths, and an immersive museum featuring giant animatronic King Kong fingers poking through faux office walls.
113.p3: Yet @BadCallBobby rode those high-speed Otis elevators expecting a Major League Baseball rules committee, leaving a furious review titled "You're OUT-ragous!" because the "Umpire State Building" was "just one giant, yelling sports official" where every call was questioned. Confusing a twelve-hundred-and-fifty-foot Art Deco masterpiece on Fifth Avenue with a grumpy man in a chest protector behind home plate is a swing and a miss of historic proportions. If you start screaming at the uniformed security guards on the eighty-sixth-floor promenade about a blown strike-three call at Yankee Stadium, they will happily eject you back down to Thirty-Fourth Street.
113.visitor_tip: Buy a sunset-slot ticket several days ahead online, ignore the uniformed street hawkers outside on Fifth Avenue selling fake 'express' passes, and bring a windbreaker even in July.

114.headline: Two-Thousand-Year-Old Nabataean Sandstone Facades That Refuse to Roll Over or Fetch a Stick
114.p1: Beginning around the fourth century BCE, an enterprising Arab nomadic tribe called the Nabataeans grew phenomenally wealthy by taxing caravans carrying frankincense and myrrh across the Jordanian desert, and then hid their capital inside a box canyon reachable only through a three-quarter-mile tectonic split in the sandstone cliffs. Because the region gets only six inches of rain a year, Nabataean engineers built a brilliant network of terracotta pipes, check dams, and rock-cut cisterns along the Siq gorge that prevented flash floods while supplying water for thirty thousand people and lush public gardens. After Rome annexed the kingdom in 106 CE and an earthquake leveled half the freestanding streets in 363 CE, Petra sat largely forgotten by the outside world until Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt disguised himself as an Indian scholar in 1812 and talked a local guide into showing him the Treasury.
114.p2: Visiting the Rose City today is not a quick curbside photo stop; it is a ten-mile desert hike disguised as an archaeological park. Once you walk down the narrow, two-hundred-foot-high walls of the Siq and emerge before the hundred-and-twenty-foot carved facade of Al-Khazneh (the Treasury), you step into a dust-choked circus of Bedouin touts wearing eyeliner like Jack Sparrow, boys selling postcards, and influencers posing on rented camels. If you want to see the even larger Monastery (Ad-Deir), you face an eight-hundred-and-fifty-step climb up a rocky mountain trail while dodging fast-moving donkeys whose handlers promise they are "air-conditioned mountain taxis."
114.p3: All that carved rose-red sandstone left @BoulderBummed cold, prompting a review titled "Absolutely Rock Bottom Experience!" that complained this "ancient companion" from the desert "just sits there, completely unresponsive" and never once wagged its tail. Flying all the way to the Wadi Musa valley in southern Jordan because you thought the ancient city of Petra was a 1970s novelty "Pet Rock" in a cardboard box with breathing holes is a staggering geographical misfire. You cannot teach a forty-meter Hellenistic-style sandstone royal tomb to play fetch, and rubbing its nose will only get you scolded by the Jordanian tourist police.
114.visitor_tip: Enter through the gate at six in the morning to photograph the Treasury before the camel handlers arrive, and never pay to go 'inside' the Treasury since it is a roped-off empty stone cube.

115.headline: Fifty Million Watts of Midtown Neon and Aggressive Elmos With Not a Single Sonnet in Sight
115.p1: Until 1904, the bowtie intersection where Broadway slashes diagonally across Seventh Avenue in Manhattan was a gritty carriage-and-horse district called Longacre Square, dominated by harness shops and William H. Vanderbilt's American Horse Exchange. Everything changed when publisher Adolph Ochs moved the headquarters of The New York Times into a narrow twenty-five-story tower at Forty-Second Street and persuaded Mayor George B. McClellan Jr. to rename the plaza and its new subway station Times Square. By the 1920s, zoning rules actually required buildings in the district to maintain massive illuminated signage to keep the theatrical energy alive, a mandate that survived the sleazy grindhouse cinema decades of the 1970s to become the hyper-commercial canyon of high-definition LED billboards we know today.
115.p2: Standing in the middle of Father Duffy Square in the twenty-first century feels like climbing inside a giant pinball machine during a blackout testing drill. Even at three in the morning, fifty-story-tall digital screens blast advertisements for prescription pharmaceuticals, fast fashion, and Broadway musicals at eyeball-searing brightness while steam hisses up through orange plastic Con Edison chimneys in the asphalt. On the pavement below, three hundred thousand daily pedestrians weave around unlicensed costumed characters in slightly mildewed Spider-Man and Elmo suits who aggressively demand twenty-dollar tips the second a confused tourist raises a smartphone camera.
115.p3: Into this sensory blender stepped @StanzaSlammer, who wrote "Utterly lacking in poetic justice!" to complain that "Rhymes Square" offered "not a single rhyming couplet" on any of its flashing screens. Traveling to Forty-Second Street expecting a quiet outdoor literary salon where billboards project iambic pentameter is like showing up at the Super Bowl hoping for a harp recital. While Tin Pan Alley composers certainly cranked out plenty of rhyming lyrics a few blocks south in the early nineteen-hundreds, the only verses you will hear in Times Square today involve a guy in a knockoff Batman cape demanding cash or threatening to delete your vacation photo.
115.visitor_tip: Keep walking if anyone tries to hand you a 'free' autographed CD or offers a photo with a cartoon character, and use the red TKTS glass steps at the north end for discounted same-day Broadway tickets.

116.headline: Nine Miles of Former Royal Palace Galleries That Will Not Exfoliate Your Elbows
116.p1: Before it held thirty-eight thousand works of art, the Louvre was a grim twelfth-century stone fortress built by King Philip II in 1190 to stop Viking and English raiders from sailing up the Seine while he was away on the Third Crusade. You can still walk down into the basement today and see the original medieval moat piers that Renaissance kings later buried beneath sprawling royal apartments. When Louis XIV grew tired of rebellious Parisian mobs in 1682 and moved his entire court out to Versailles, the abandoned palace briefly became a chaotic squatters' village for artists and stove-piped workshops until the French Revolutionaries nationalized the royal art collection and opened the building as a public museum in August 1793.
116.p2: Entering that collection today starts in the Cour Napoléon, where tourists spend forty minutes taking forced-perspective photos pinching the tip of I. M. Pei's 1989 glass pyramid before descending into an underground shopping mall aroma of espresso and damp raincoats. With over four hundred rooms spread across three enormous wings, the Louvre is less an afternoon stroll and more a forced march through European history. Ninety percent of visitors sprint directly past five thousand years of Mesopotamian antiquities and Delacroix canvases to pack ten-deep into the Salle des États, where they hold phones above their heads to snap a blurry three-inch photo of the Mona Lisa behind two panes of bulletproof glass.
116.p3: That artistic marathon left @ScrubbieDoo with an unusual dermatological complaint in "Left feeling completely unsmoothed.", grieving that the "Loofah Museum" was full of "scratchy fibers" and left their skin "scrubbed raw." Showing up on the Right Bank of Paris in a bathrobe expecting the world's largest art museum to be a showroom for fibrous shower sponges is a monumental failure of French pronunciation. We can only hope @ScrubbieDoo did not attempt to exfoliate their shoulders against the Winged Victory of Samothrace or Jacques-Louis David's twenty-by-thirty-foot canvas of the Coronation of Napoleon before security escorted them to the Rue de Rivoli.
116.visitor_tip: Skip the long outdoor line at the central glass pyramid and enter through the underground Carrousel du Louvre shopping gallery on Rue de Rivoli with a pre-booked timed ticket.

117.headline: Thirteen Centuries of Tidal Granite and Benedictine Cloisters That Are Not an ICBM Silo
117.p1: According to medieval church tradition, Mont Saint-Michel began in 708 CE when the Archangel Michael appeared to Bishop Aubert of Avranches in three separate dreams and ordered him to build a sanctuary atop a lonely granite outcrop in the Couesnon river mouth; when Aubert hesitated twice, the archangel reportedly poked a hole straight through the bishop's skull with a glowing finger to make his point. Over the next eight hundred years, Benedictine monks hauled granite blocks across the treacherous tidal mudflats to construct a vertiginous Gothic abbey balanced straight on the peak of the rock, which proved so impregnable during the Hundred Years' War that the English never captured it, and so inescapable that King Louis XI and later Napoleon turned the monastery into a high-security prison.
117.p2: Visiting the mount today requires timing your arrival against the strongest tides in continental Europe, which surge across the flat bay thirteen miles outward at the speed of a galloping horse. Since 2014, a sleek elevated bridge has replaced the old nineteenth-century causeway so tidal currents can flush out decades of accumulated silt. Once you ride the shuttle bus across and pass through the medieval King's Gate, you join three million annual visitors squeezing up the single narrow cobblestone street of the Grande Rue, where servers at La Mère Poulard rhythmically beat forty-euro soufflé omelets in copper bowls while seagulls the size of small terriers dive-bomb anyone carrying a butter biscuit.
117.p3: Despite thirteen hundred years of monastic architecture, @BlastOffBeth left a one-star review titled "Detonation Disappointment!" after arriving on the Normandy coast expecting "Mont Saint-Missile" to feature a "launch sequence, not Gregorian chants." Driving four hours west of Paris in hopes of watching a medieval granite island blast off into low Earth orbit like a Saturn V rocket is an astonishing misreading of French heritage. While the needle-thin 1897 spire topped by a gilded copper statue of St. Michael slaying a dragon certainly points five hundred and fifteen feet into the sky like a nosecone, the island remains firmly bolted to the Normandy bedrock.
117.visitor_tip: Stay overnight at one of the small hotels on the island or near the dam so you can walk the abbey ramparts after five in the evening when the day-trip tour buses have departed.

118.headline: Twenty-Two Acres of Chilly San Francisco Bay Sandstone That Will Not Cure Your Indigestion
118.p1: When Spanish naval officer Juan Manuel de Ayala charted San Francisco Bay in 1775, he named a barren, guano-encrusted twelve-acre rock La Isla de los Alcatraces, or the Island of the Pelicans. The United States Army quickly realized the rock sat directly inside the Golden Gate shipping lane, turning it into a harbor fortress in the 1850s and a military stockade by the Civil War before transferring it to the Department of Justice in 1934 as a maximum-security federal penitentiary. Designed to hold one prisoner per five-by-nine-foot cell to prevent conspiracies, Alcatraz housed notorious inmates like Al Capone and Robert Stroud for just twenty-nine years before Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy shut it down in 1963 because salt spray was rotting the concrete and every single gallon of fresh water had to be barged across the bay.
118.p2: Getting to "The Rock" today is actually harder than it was for 1930s bank robbers, since ferry tickets from Pier 33 regularly sell out weeks in advance during the summer. After a brisk fifteen-minute boat ride through forty-degree coastal fog and fifty-five-degree tidal currents, visitors hike a quarter-mile equivalent of thirteen stories up the concrete switchbacks while breathing the rich, pungent aroma of nesting western gulls and Brandt's cormorants. Inside the drafty cellhouse, hundreds of tourists shuffle down "Broadway" in total silence because everyone is wearing headphones listening to the same award-winning audio tour narrated by actual former guards and inmates.
118.p3: That chilling maritime atmosphere failed to impress @FizzWizz, who titled their review "Definitely not a solid experience." and complained that "Alka-Seltzer Island" just "keeps fizzing away" and "only treats heartburn, doesn't hold convicts!" How a traveler books a National Park Service ferry across San Francisco Bay expecting twenty-two acres of fractured graywacke sandstone to dissolve into giant bubbles of sodium bicarbonate and citric acid is anyone's guess. In 1962, Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers famously chiseled through the moisture-damaged concrete ventilation ducts using stolen cafeteria spoons and a vacuum-cleaner motor drill, though even they never tried dissolving the prison walls like an antacid tablet.
118.visitor_tip: Book your ferry ticket exclusively through the official Alcatraz City Cruises website at least three weeks ahead, and dress in warm layers even if downtown San Francisco looks sunny.

119.headline: One Hundred and Thirty-Five Travertine Steps Built by French Diplomats With Zero Four-Way Stretch
119.p1: Rome's Spanish Steps are a monument to eighteenth-century diplomatic pettiness. For over a century, the steep muddy slope between the Piazza di Spagna (named after the nearby Spanish Embassy to the Holy See) and the French royal church of Trinità dei Monti at the top of the hill was an embarrassment to both nations. In 1660, a wealthy French diplomat named Étienne Gueffier died and left twenty thousand scudi in his will to fund a grand staircase, provided it honored the King of France. Pope Clement XI naturally objected to putting a giant statue of Louis XIV in the middle of Rome, stalling construction until 1723, when an obscure Roman architect named Francesco de Sanctis finally bridged the ninety-five-foot elevation gap with a butterfly-shaped cascade of a hundred and thirty-five travertine marble steps.
119.p2: For the next three centuries, those curved stone terraces served as Rome's favorite open-air living room, hosting everyone from nineteenth-century artists' models in regional costumes to Audrey Hepburn eating a gelato cone in Roman Holiday. That tradition came to an abrupt end in August 2019, when the Rome city council grew tired of scrubbing spilled wine and coffee off the freshly restored travertine (cleaned in 2016 with a one-point-five-million-euro donation from luxury jeweler Bulgari) and made it completely illegal to sit down on the steps. Today, white-gloved municipal police officers patrol the bottom and top landings with silver whistles, blowing shrill blasts at any tired tourist who dares to rest their backside on the stone and threatening fines of up to four hundred euros.
119.p3: That lack of yield was taken remarkably literally by @TooTightTommy, whose review, "Seriously unsupportive!", complained of "zero give in the fabric" at the "Spandex Steps" and claimed that "every single rise was a struggle... my seams just couldn't take it!" Walking out of the Spagna Metro station expecting an eighteenth-century Roman Baroque staircase to stretch around your calves like a pair of synthetic cycling shorts is a fashion crisis of historic proportions. Travertine limestone quarried from Tivoli has survived three hundred years of carriages, revolutions, and summer heat waves precisely because it has the elasticity of a brick wall.
119.visitor_tip: Look, photograph, and walk up the steps all you like, but do not sit down or eat gelato on the marble unless you want a whistle blown in your ear and a hefty municipal fine.

120.headline: Baroque Marble and Sunken Fountain Engineering in the Piazza di Spagna With Zero Leafy Iron
120.p1: At the foot of the Spanish Steps sits one of Rome's cleverest engineering compromises: the Fontana della Barcaccia, or "Fountain of the Ugly Boat," sculpted between 1627 and 1629 by Pietro Bernini and his famous son Gian Lorenzo. Because the ancient Acqua Vergine aqueduct arrived at the Piazza di Spagna with almost zero water pressure, the Berninis could not build tall, dramatic upward jets; instead, they dug a basin slightly below street level and carved a half-sunken marble barge gently overflowing with crystal-clear water, inspired by a legend of a river boat stranded in the square during the great Tiber flood of Christmas 1598. Directly to the right of the bottom steps stands the terracotta-colored Casa Rossa, where the twenty-five-year-old English Romantic poet John Keats spent his final agonizing months before dying of tuberculosis in a tiny second-floor bedroom in February 1821.
120.p2: By the late eighteenth century, this corner of Rome had collected so many homesick British aristocrats on the Grand Tour that locals nicknamed the neighborhood the "English Ghetto," a legacy preserved at Babington's Tea Rooms, founded at the left foot of the staircase in 1893 by two Victorian women who were scandalized that you couldn't buy proper tea in Italy. In spring, the municipal parks department lines the central stone ramps with hundreds of potted pink and white azaleas, drawing dense crowds of shoppers spilling out of the luxury flagship boutiques on Via Condotti. Navigating the lower piazza requires dodging persistent street hawkers who try to shove a long-stemmed red rose into your hand and then demand five euros while claiming it was a free gift for your spouse.
120.p3: None of this Romantic poetry or seventeenth-century hydraulic cleverness satisfied @WiltedGreens, who filed "Not the power boost I expected." after climbing the "Spinach Steps" and complaining of "endless, unseasoned leafy horror" with no Popeye in sight. How a traveler books a flight to Leonardo da Vinci Airport expecting Rome's grandest Baroque urban staircase to be a giant steamed pile of iron-rich dark leafy vegetables is a culinary mystery for the ages. If you see anything green on the staircase outside of the April azalea festival, it is merely moss growing near the Bernini fountain spouts, and you should not put olive oil on it.
120.visitor_tip: Refill your water bottle for free from the brass spouts of Bernini's Barcaccia fountain (which runs with cold, potable Acqua Vergine water), and visit the peaceful Keats-Shelley House museum right beside the steps.
